props.title: Cornered
props.initialSlug: Trapped in a web of deceit.

sections.content: Cornered stands as a crucial post-WWII noir that captures the raw anger and disillusionment of returning veterans. Director Edward Dmytryk, fresh off his success with Murder, My Sweet (1944), crafts a revenge thriller that's darker and more politically charged than most films of its era. Dick Powell, continuing his transformation from song-and-dance man to hardboiled actor, delivers a searing performance as a Canadian airman hunting his wife's killers through the streets of Buenos Aires. The film's exploration of Nazi collaborators hiding in South America preceded later masterpieces like The Boys from Brazil (1978) and Marathon Man (1976).

sections.content: The film's Buenos Aires setting wasn't just exotic window dressing - it reflected real concerns about Nazi escape routes through South America. Dmytryk and screenwriter John Paxton inject palpable fury into every frame, with Powell's character Laurence Gerard embodying the vengeful spirit of a generation scarred by war. The cinematography by Harry J. Wild emphasizes claustrophobic interiors and canted angles that would influence later South American-set noirs like Out of the Past (1947) and Lady from Shanghai (1947).

Cornered marked a significant evolution in Dick Powell's career, building on his noir debut in Murder, My Sweet (1944). His portrayal of Gerard shows none of the witty charm of his Philip Marlowe - instead, he's a damaged man consumed by hatred. This psychological complexity predates similar veteran-seeking-revenge narratives like Act of Violence (1948) and Rolling Thunder (1977). SUBHEAD: Political Context and Legacy

sections.content: The film's production coincided with the House Un-American Activities Committee's rising influence in Hollywood. Dmytryk would later be blacklisted as one of the Hollywood Ten, making Cornered's anti-fascist themes especially poignant. The film's unflinching look at post-war political intrigue influenced later conspiracy thrillers like The Day of the Jackal (1973) and Three Days of the Condor (1975).
